scenes.title: One meal too many
scenes.viewerPurpose: Feel how one appetite can leave another person hungry Connect the book’s title with the cost carried by others Recognize these as stories from living traditions
scenes.composition: Finite winter food is shared among ordinary people
addOrChange: Add no antlers, invented ritual or stereotyped costume.

cues.narration: In a winter camp, taking more than your share can mean someone else does not eat.
cues.visualAction: One portion grows while someone else’s portion shrinks.

cues.narration: Wendigo begins with that stark relationship between appetite and the people who bear its cost.
cues.visualAction: Keep people attached to the food as the book is named.

cues.narration: It approaches this figure from living Anishinaabe traditions, with care for the people whose stories these are.
cues.visualAction: Remain with the human shared setting and respect its specific cultural origin.

scenes.title: The appetite that grows
scenes.viewerPurpose: Ask whether the pattern appears in ordinary organizations See growth becoming the next day’s minimum
scenes.composition: A modern organization sets a larger target after success
addOrChange: Replace appetite symbols with orders, work and an ordinary planning desk.

cues.narration: Then it asks whether a similar hunger can grow inside ordinary modern organizations.
cues.visualAction: Move from shared provisions to a modern expansion decision.

cues.narration: A company expands, a platform seeks attention, and yesterday’s success becomes tomorrow’s minimum.
cues.visualAction: Yesterday’s completed target becomes the new minimum.

scenes.title: The distant cost
scenes.viewerPurpose: Notice that harmful pressure does not require conscious greed Feel how distance hides another life’s loss Connect the stories to business and technology
scenes.composition: A product reaches a customer while costs fall on distant work and land
addOrChange: Use one necessary supply relation instead of a consuming monster.

cues.narration: The people inside these systems need not think of themselves as greedy.
cues.visualAction: Show ordinary people carrying out locally reasonable tasks.

cues.narration: Distance can hide the connection between what is gained and what another life loses.
cues.visualAction: Widen along the supply relation to the previously unseen person.

cues.narration: The book connects these stories with business, technology, and the difficulty of choosing when to stop.
cues.visualAction: Bring gain and cost into the same understandable view.

scenes.title: When enough can count
scenes.viewerPurpose: Carry the question beyond its winter setting Ask how a successful system could recognize enough
scenes.composition: A fulfilled need remains beside a living landscape
addOrChange: Use enough as a small question on a decision note, not a victory slogan.

cues.narration: Its unsettling question stays recognizable far beyond a winter story.
cues.visualAction: Recall the shared winter provision beside the modern transaction.

cues.narration: What happens when a successful system cannot recognize enough?
cues.visualAction: Hold the option to stop expanding without erasing the landscape.
